opus-5.5.text:
I think scepticism is one of the most important skills in this field. Honestly, it might be *the* most important one.

The core problem with interpretability is that it's very easy to fool yourself. You're looking at a model with billions of parameters, you have some hypothesis about what it's doing, and you find evidence that seems to fit. Humans are extremely good at pattern-matching and telling compelling stories. Neural networks are extremely good at being weird and messy in ways that don't fit those stories. So the default outcome, if you're not careful, is that you produce something that looks like a beautiful explanation but is subtly or badly wrong.

I've seen this happen a lot, including in my own work. You find a neuron that seems to fire on, say, French text, and you get excited and call it the "French neuron." Then you look more carefully and it's also firing on a bunch of other things. Or it's only part of the story and the model has five other ways of doing the same thing. Or your probe found a direction that correlates with the concept, but the model doesn't actually use that direction. There are so many ways for an interpretation to be an illusion.

So in practice, scepticism looks like a few things for me. First, constantly asking "what else could explain this?" and actively trying to falsify your own hypothesis rather than collecting confirming evidence. Second, preferring causal interventions over purely correlational evidence. If you think a component does X, ablate it or patch it and check that the behaviour changes the way you'd predict. Third, sanity checks and baselines. Does your technique also find "interpretable" structure in a randomly initialised model? If so, that's a bad sign. And fourth, being honest about how much of the behaviour your explanation actually accounts for, rather than explaining the easy 60% and quietly ignoring the rest.

I'd also say scepticism should apply at the level of the field, not just individual papers. Interpretability has had a bunch of hype cycles where a technique looks really promising and everyone piles in, and then a couple of years later people realise it has significant limitations. I think it's healthy to hold our tools to a high standard and ask, "Does this actually help us do something useful that we couldn't do otherwise?" That's the real test. Can it help us detect deception, debug a model, or predict behaviour better than simpler baselines? If an interpretability method can't beat a dumb baseline on a real task, that's important to know.

That said, I don't want scepticism to tip into paralysis. You need some willingness to form bold hypotheses and run with them, especially early in exploratory work. The skill is to hold your ideas loosely: be creative when generating hypotheses, be ruthless when evaluating them, and be clear with yourself and your readers about which mode you're in.

r001.rationale: The response frames scepticism as checking whether evidence supports an interpretation before accepting it, using falsification, causal interventions, and baselines to test claims.

r002.rationale: It recommends actively trying to falsify one’s own hypothesis instead of collecting only confirming evidence, including when one is excited about an interpretation.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think scepticism is maybe the single most important skill in mech interp, and it's also the thing the field has historically been worst at. Let me explain what I mean.

The core problem is that interpretability is a field where it is incredibly easy to fool yourself. You look at a model, you find some neuron or some feature or some circuit, you stare at the examples it activates on, and your brain is extremely good at pattern-matching and telling you a story. "Oh, this is the 'legal language' neuron," or "this attention head is doing induction." And the story feels compelling, and you write it up, and it might just be wrong. Or, more insidiously, it might be sort of right but massively oversimplified, and the simplified story is what gets remembered.

And there's a long history of this. People found "grandmother neurons" in vision models that turned out to be polysemantic. People found beautiful clean explanations of circuits that explained maybe 30 or 40 percent of what the model was actually doing on that task, and the rest was a mess that nobody talked about. I've done this myself. I've had results where I was pretty excited and then someone ran a slightly different control and the effect halved.

So the way I think about it is: your job as an interpretability researcher is to be the harshest critic of your own work. Every time you have a hypothesis about what a model is doing, you should ask, "What would I expect to see if this were false? Have I actually checked that?" Causal interventions are a big part of this. If you think a feature represents some concept, don't just look at the activations, go and ablate it, or steer with it, and see if the model's behaviour changes in the way you predict. If you think a circuit does a task, measure how much of the model's performance you actually recover when you only use that circuit. Have baselines. Have controls. Try to break your own result before someone else does.

And I want to be clear that this cuts both ways. Scepticism isn't just "be pessimistic about interpretability." There's a version of this that's lazy, where people say "the model is just a big inscrutable matrix, nothing is really interpretable," and I think that's also a failure of scepticism, because it's not engaging with the evidence either. We genuinely have found real, robust structure in models. Induction heads are real. Some sparse autoencoder features are real and clean and do what they look like they do. The point isn't to disbelieve everything, it's to calibrate. Believe things in proportion to the evidence, and be honest about where the evidence is thin.

The other thing I'd say is that this really matters for the safety case. If the pitch for interpretability is "we'll be able to look inside a model and check whether it's being deceptive or has some dangerous goal," then the failure mode that keeps me up at night is not "interpretability doesn't work." It's "interpretability sort of works, we have tools that give us a confident-looking answer, and the answer is wrong, and we trusted it." A false sense of security is worse than no tool at all. So building a culture where people are rigorous and sceptical and where it's normal to publish "we tried X and it didn't work" or "this result was weaker than it looked" is, I think, load-bearing for the whole project.

So yeah, if I had to give one piece of advice to someone entering the field, it'd be: fall in love with the question of whether you're wrong, not with your hypothesis.

r001.rationale: The response says to calibrate belief to the evidence and asks whether a hypothesis has been tested against evidence that could show it is false.

r002.rationale: It advises researchers to be the harshest critics of their own work, try to break their results, and focus on whether they are wrong rather than becoming attached to a hypothesis.

astra-6.text:
I think scepticism is incredibly important, particularly scepticism about your own explanations. In mechanistic interpretability, you look inside a model, find something that looks interesting, and try to tell a story about what it’s doing. And it’s very easy to find a story that sounds convincing without actually having identified the mechanism.

The question I want to ask is: how would I know if this explanation were wrong? What predictions does it make? Can I intervene on the model in a way where my explanation predicts one outcome and a plausible alternative predicts another? If I think a particular component is doing something important, can I change what it’s doing and get the corresponding change in the model’s behaviour?

Even then, you need to be careful. An intervention might break the model in some unrelated way. So you want controls, different examples, and a sense of where your explanation stops working.

But I think there’s a useful distinction between scepticism that helps you design a better experiment and scepticism that just says, ‘Well, neural networks are complicated, so we can’t understand anything.’ The former is essential. You can make progress without having a complete explanation, as long as you’re precise about what the evidence actually supports.

r001.rationale: The response says to test explanations against predictions and interventions, then be precise about what the evidence supports. This presents scepticism as assessing whether evidence justifies confidence in an explanation.

r002.rationale: It encourages questioning one’s own explanations and considering alternatives, but does not mention becoming attached to a hypothesis or deliberately seeking flaws because of that attachment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think scepticism is incredibly important, especially because it’s very easy to find a story about what a neural network is doing that feels compelling. You look at a few examples, you see a pattern, and suddenly you feel like you understand the mechanism. But a plausible story is a hypothesis, and you need to work out how to test it.

So I want to ask: what would I expect to see if this explanation were wrong? Can I intervene on the network and change its behaviour in the way my explanation predicts? Does the explanation hold up on examples I didn’t use to develop it? And am I explaining the actual computation, or have I just found something correlated with it?

There’s also a balance here. If your standard is that you won’t investigate anything until you’re certain it’s real, you won’t get very far. Exploring patterns and forming speculative hypotheses is useful. The important thing is to keep track of the difference between ‘this is an interesting possibility’ and ‘we have strong evidence for this.’ Ideally, scepticism is what helps you turn the first into the second.

r001.rationale: The response says to test explanations against interventions and new examples, then distinguish an interesting possibility from one supported by strong evidence. This communicates judging whether the evidence justifies greater confidence.

r002.rationale: The response recommends asking what would be expected if an explanation were wrong and testing it, but does not address deliberately seeking flaws in hypotheses the researcher has become attached to.
